verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. There is no Lean definition named for F_slow as an operator on a triple (u,p,T); the combination appears inline in the statement of finite_error_rate as navierStokesResidual u p - prefixStressForce, and the two sign conventions compose to the paper's formula. Term by term: R(u,p) is navierStokesResidual, which is ∂_t u + (u·∇)u - Δu + ∇p, matching (3.1) at viscosity one. radialDivergence k S = √(2s)·∂_s S + k·S/√(2s); since s = r²/2 gives ∂_r = r ∂_s = √(2s) ∂_s and √(2·radialEnergy x) = √(x0²+x1²) = r (AxisymmetricFields.radialEnergy x = (x0²+x1²)/2), this is exactly (∂_r + k/r)S, with k = 2 on the θ stress and k = 1 on the z stress as in the paper. The sign: tangentialStressForce packs the Cartesian vector (x1·a/r, -x0·a/r, -z), and the Lean azimuthal direction is e_θ = (-x1, x0, 0)/r (the comment and components of AxisymmetricResidual.velocity, NavierStokes/AxisymmetricResidual.lean:262, give angular velocity r·F contributing (-x1·F, x0·F, 0)), so tangentialStressForce = -[(∂_r+2/r)T_θ e_θ + (∂_r+1/r)T_z e_z]; it is then subtracted, and the two minus signs cancel, so the statement's field is literally F_slow(u,p,T). Remaining difference is packaging: the stress pair T = (T_θ, T_z) is carried as two separate scalar profile arguments, not a pair, and F_slow is never applied to a general triple under one name.
